title: UML for interviews
scopeHtml: Scope: class, sequence, state, use-case and activity diagrams, mapping each to code, and how to draw them fast in an LLD interview.

notes.title: Why UML in interviews
notes.html:
UML is a shared drawing language for software. In an LLD interview you do not need the full standard; you need 5 quick sketches that show structure (class), behaviour over time (sequence), life of one object (state), who-uses-what (use-case) and workflow (activity).

The rule: draw the smallest diagram that answers the question. Interviewers judge clarity and speed, not UML purity. Plan on 2 minutes for a class diagram and 1 minute for a sequence diagram.

Worked example. Design a parking lot in 45 minutes: 3 min requirements, 2 min use-case list, 6 min class diagram, 3 min sequence for "park a car", 1 min state for a ticket, then 25 min code. Without drawing, candidates often spend 15 minutes confused about relationships.

Industry examples. Teams use PlantUML and Mermaid text diagrams in pull requests; Android docs show architecture as boxes and arrows; Uber and Netflix tech blogs use sequence-like flows. Few teams keep heavy UML tools, but all sketch.

Everyday analogy. A map, a recipe and a flowchart all describe the same city or meal from different angles. You pick the one that answers the question.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing everything at once. Ask "structure or flow?" and draw one.
  • Spending 10 minutes on notation details nobody asked for.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
A class diagram shows classes, their fields and methods, and how they relate. It is the main LLD artifact.

Box with 3 compartments: name, attributes, methods. Visibility: + public, - private, # protected.

Relationships, from weakest to strongest:

Association        A ------> B     A knows/uses B (field or parameter)
Dependency         A - - - > B     A uses B briefly (method parameter, local)
Aggregation        A <>----- B     A has B, B can live alone (Team has Players)
Composition        A <#>---- B     A owns B, B dies with A (House has Rooms)
Inheritance        A ------|> B    A is a B (extends)
Realization        A - - -|> B     A implements interface B
Multiplicity       1, 0..1, *, 1..*   on the line ends
+---------------------+          +--------------------+
| <<interface>>       |          | ParkingLot         |
| PricingStrategy     |          |--------------------|
|---------------------|          | -floors: List<Floor>|
| +cost(Ticket): Money|          | +park(Vehicle): Ticket|
+---------------------+          +--------------------+
        ^  (realizes)                    | 1
        |                                | owns  (composition)
+---------------------+                  v *
| HourlyPricing       |          +--------------------+
+---------------------+          | Floor              |
                                 +--------------------+
interface PricingStrategy { Money cost(Ticket t); }
class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy { public Money cost(Ticket t){ return new Money(0); } }
class ParkingLot { private final List<Floor> floors = new ArrayList<>(); Ticket park(Vehicle v){ return null; } }
interface PricingStrategy { fun cost(t: Ticket): Money }
class ParkingLot { private val floors = mutableListOf<Floor>(); fun park(v: Vehicle): Ticket = TODO() }

How it maps to code. Composition = field created and owned inside (new Floor() in the constructor). Aggregation = field passed in from outside. Realization = implements. Inheritance = extends.

Fast method. (1) Underline nouns in requirements = candidate classes. (2) Verbs = methods. (3) Add <<interface>> where behaviour varies. (4) Mark multiplicities. (5) Stop at 6 to 10 classes.

Worked example. "Library: members borrow books, max 5 books, fine after 14 days." Classes: Member, Book, Loan (association class holding dates), Library, FinePolicy. Member 1 --- * Loan * --- 1 Book.

Industry examples. Android Room entity relationships (one-to-many) and Kotlin domain models map directly to class diagrams.

Everyday analogy. A family tree plus an org chart: who is part of whom and who answers to whom.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up aggregation and composition. Say it by lifecycle: "does the part die with the whole?".
  • Arrows reversed on inheritance: the arrowhead points to the PARENT.
  • Showing getters and setters; skip them, show behaviour.

notes.title: Sequence diagram
notes.html:
A sequence diagram shows who calls whom, in what order, over time. Objects are columns, time goes down.

Elements: lifeline (vertical line), solid arrow (call), dashed arrow (return), alt box (if/else), loop box, opt box (optional).

Client      Controller     OrderService     PaymentGateway     Repo
  |  placeOrder() |              |                 |             |
  |-------------->|              |                 |             |
  |               | create(o)    |                 |             |
  |               |------------->|                 |             |
  |               |              | charge(card,500)|             |
  |               |              |---------------->|             |
  |               |              |      ok         |             |
  |               |              |<- - - - - - - - |             |
  |               |              | save(o)         |             |
  |               |              |------------------------------>|
  |               |    Order     |                 |             |
  |<- - - - - - - |<- - - - - - -|                 |             |
 alt [charge fails] -> OrderService returns Error, no save

How to draw fast. Pick the one scenario (happy path), list 4 to 5 participants left to right in call order, number the arrows 1 to n, add ONE alt box for the main failure.

Order place(Cart c) {              // matches the diagram above
    payment.charge(c.card(), c.total());
    return repo.save(new Order(c));
}

Worked example. Login with OTP: App -> AuthService: requestOtp; AuthService -> SmsProvider: send; AuthService -> Cache: store(otp, TTL 5 min); App -> AuthService: verify(otp); alt wrong OTP 3 times -> lock account for 15 min.

Industry examples. Stripe and Razorpay payment docs publish sequence diagrams of authorize and capture. OAuth 2.0 docs are sequence diagrams.

Everyday analogy. A script of a play: who speaks to whom, in order.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing every internal call; show only the calls that matter to the question.
  • Forgetting the return and failure path.
  • Mixing sync and async arrows (open arrowhead means async).

notes.title: State diagram
notes.html:
A state diagram shows the states one object can be in and which events move it between them. Use it whenever an entity has a lifecycle: order, ticket, vending machine, elevator, connection.

Parts: states (rounded boxes), transitions (event [guard] / action), start dot, end dot.

 (*) --> [Created] --pay--> [Paid] --ship--> [Shipped] --deliver--> [Delivered] --> (*)
            |                  |
          cancel             cancel [within 24h]
            v                  v
        [Cancelled] <----------+
enum OrderState {
    CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;
    boolean canGoTo(OrderState next) {
        return switch (this) {
            case CREATED -> next == PAID || next == CANCELLED;
            case PAID -> next == SHIPPED || next == CANCELLED;
            case SHIPPED -> next == DELIVERED;
            default -> false;
        };
    }
}
enum class OrderState {
    CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;
    fun canGoTo(n: OrderState) = when (this) {
        CREATED -> n == PAID || n == CANCELLED
        PAID -> n == SHIPPED || n == CANCELLED
        SHIPPED -> n == DELIVERED
        else -> false
    }
}

Code mapping. Simple: enum plus a canGoTo table. Rich behaviour per state: State pattern (interface State, one class per state). Big workflows: a state machine library.

Worked example. Vending machine: Idle -> (coin) HasMoney -> (select, stock>0) Dispensing -> Idle. Illegal moves (dispense with no money) are exactly the cells missing from the table, which also gives your test cases.

Industry examples. Order status in Swiggy/Zomato (placed, accepted, picked up, delivered), Stripe PaymentIntent states, TCP connection states, Android Activity lifecycle.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light or a parcel tracking page: only certain next steps are legal.

Common interview traps.

  • Missing the illegal transitions; say what happens on an unexpected event (ignore or throw).
  • Forgetting concurrency: two threads paying and cancelling at once need a lock or compare-and-set on the state.

notes.title: Use-case diagram
notes.html:
A use-case diagram shows who (actors) uses the system for what (use cases), nothing about how. It is the requirements picture, usually the first minute of an LLD interview.

Stick figures = actors, ovals = use cases, box = system boundary. <<include>> means always happens as part of another; <<extend>> means optional addition.

              +------------- ATM System -------------+
 Customer --> | (Withdraw cash) --<<include>>--> (Authenticate PIN) |
 Customer --> | (Check balance) --<<include>>--> (Authenticate PIN) |
 Customer --> | (Deposit)       <--<<extend>>--- (Print receipt)    |
 Bank staff-> | (Refill cash)                          |
              +----------------------------------------+

Fast method. List actors (human or external system) in 30 seconds, then 4 to 6 verbs per actor. Each use case later becomes a public method or a test case.

Worked example. Ride booking: Rider (request ride, cancel, rate), Driver (accept, start trip, end trip), Payment system (charge). Each oval becomes a service method such as requestRide(riderId, pickup, drop).

Industry examples. Product requirement docs at Uber/Ola start from user journeys; Agile user stories ("As a rider I want...") are textual use cases.

Everyday analogy. A menu that lists what each type of customer can order, without the recipe.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting implementation detail (database, classes) in a use-case diagram.
  • Confusing include and extend direction.
  • Forgetting external actors such as a payment gateway or scheduler.

notes.title: Activity diagram
notes.html:
An activity diagram is a flowchart for a process: steps, decisions, parallel branches. Use it for workflows such as checkout, refund approval or CI pipelines.

Symbols: filled dot start, rounded box action, diamond decision, thick bar fork/join (parallel), swimlanes (who does it).

(*) -> [Validate cart] -> <in stock?> --no--> [Show error] -> (end)
                              |yes
                              v
                 ===fork===> [Charge card]  ||  [Reserve stock] ===join===
                                              v
                                       [Send confirmation] -> (end)

Mapping to code. Decisions = if; fork = parallel calls (CompletableFuture.allOf / coroutines async); swimlanes = classes or services.

suspend fun checkout(c: Cart) = coroutineScope {
    val pay = async { gateway.charge(c) }
    val stock = async { inventory.reserve(c) }
    pay.await(); stock.await()
}

Worked example. Charge (800 ms) and reserve stock (300 ms) in parallel take about 800 ms instead of 1,100 ms in sequence, but now you must handle one succeeding and the other failing (compensate by refunding or releasing).

Everyday analogy. A recipe card with "while the pasta boils, make the sauce".

Common interview traps.

  • Using it where a sequence diagram (who calls whom) fits better.
  • Parallel steps with no failure or rollback story.

notes.title: Drawing fast in an interview
notes.html:
Order of drawing (about 6 minutes total)
1. Use-case list (text, 1 min)       -> scope
2. Class diagram (2 min)             -> nouns, interfaces, 1..* marks
3. Sequence of the main flow (1.5)   -> proves the classes work together
4. State diagram if an entity has a lifecycle (1)
5. Say what you skipped, then code

Tips that save time: use short names; skip getters/setters/types unless asked; draw interfaces first and mark them <<interface>>; number sequence arrows; write multiplicities only where they matter; ask "may I use Mermaid-like ASCII or boxes?" and keep the same notation throughout.

Mermaid (text) is often accepted on shared screens:
classDiagram
  ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" Floor
  PricingStrategy <|.. HourlyPricing

Worked example. At 5 minutes: 7 classes, 2 interfaces, one sequence. The interviewer interrupts to add "and discounts": you add a DiscountPolicy interface in 10 seconds because the diagram showed where the seam is.

Decision gravity. Diagrams are cheap and reversible; redrawing at minute 5 beats refactoring code at minute 35.

Everyday analogy. An architect's napkin sketch before the blueprint.

Common interview traps.

  • Perfecting the diagram and having no time to code.
  • Never connecting the diagram to code; always say which class implements which box.
  • Silent drawing; narrate your reasoning.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Five diagrams: class (structure), sequence (calls over time), state (lifecycle), use-case (who does what), activity (workflow).
  • Relationships: dependency < association < aggregation < composition; inheritance = extends (arrow to parent), realization = implements.
  • Ask "does the part die with the whole?" to choose composition vs aggregation.
  • State diagrams become an enum plus transition table; list illegal transitions as tests.
  • Draw order: use-cases, classes, one sequence, state if needed, then code.
  • Be quick, narrate, skip getters/setters, and link every box to code.

questions.promptHtml: In an LLD interview, which UML diagrams do you actually draw, and how do you pick one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They judge clarity and speed, not notation purity; picking the right sketch shows judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Five sketches: class diagram for structure, sequence for calls over time, state for one object's lifecycle, use-case for who does what, activity for a workflow. I pick by the question: structure means class, order of calls means sequence, lifecycle means state. I draw the smallest one that answers it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Budget about 2 minutes for a class diagram and 1 for a sequence. In a 45-minute parking-lot design: 3 min requirements, 2 min use-cases, 6 min class diagram, 3 min sequence for "park a car", 1 min state for a ticket, then about 25 min code. Without drawing, candidates often spend 15 minutes confused about relationships.

Structure?  -> class diagram
Call order? -> sequence diagram
Lifecycle?  -> state diagram
Who uses?   -> use-case diagram
Workflow?   -> activity diagram

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Drawing everything at once; ask "structure or flow?".
  • Spending 10 minutes on notation nobody asked for.
  • Silent drawing; narrate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do you need strict UML? -> No, consistent boxes and arrows are enough.
  2. Can you use Mermaid? -> Often accepted on shared screens; ask first.
  3. What do you skip when short on time? -> Use-case and activity; keep class and one sequence.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE draws one big diagram. Senior chooses per question, time-boxes and ties each box to code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams keep PlantUML or Mermaid in pull requests so a design review has a picture.

questions.promptHtml: In a class diagram, what is the difference between association, aggregation and composition, and how do they show up in code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most-confused part of UML; the lifecycle test shows real understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Association: A knows or uses B (field or parameter). Aggregation: A has B but B can live alone, like Team and Players. Composition: A owns B and B dies with A, like House and Rooms. I choose by asking "does the part die with the whole?".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strength order: dependency < association < aggregation < composition; inheritance is extends with the arrow to the parent, realization is implements with a dashed arrow. In code, composition is a field created and owned inside (new Floor() in the constructor); aggregation is a field passed in from outside.

A - - -> B   dependency (parameter, local)
A ------> B  association (field)
A <>----- B  aggregation (B lives alone)
A <#>---- B  composition (B dies with A)
A ------|> B inheritance (arrow to parent)
A - - -|> B  realization (implements)

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class House { private final List<Room> rooms = new ArrayList<>(); House() { rooms.add(new Room()); } }   // composition
class Team  { private final List<Player> players; Team(List<Player> p) { players = p; } }              // aggregation
class House { private val rooms = mutableListOf(Room()) }          // composition
class Team(private val players: List<Player>)                      // aggregation

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing aggregation and composition; use the lifecycle question.
  • Inheritance arrow reversed.
  • Showing getters and setters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Arrow for implementing an interface? -> Dashed line, hollow triangle to the interface.
  2. When do you use dependency? -> A short-lived use, a parameter or local.
  3. Does a UML aggregation have runtime impact? -> No, it is a modelling intent expressed by who creates and owns the object.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE memorises the diamonds. Senior reads them from ownership and lifecycle in code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Reviewing a ParkingLot design, "Floor lives alone?" settled whether floors could be shared between lots.

questions.promptHtml: How do you turn a state diagram into code, and when do you choose an enum versus the State pattern?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many entities (order, ticket, elevator) have lifecycles; interviewers want legal transitions and concurrency awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A state diagram lists states and the events that move between them. Simple case: an enum with a canGoTo table. If each state has rich behaviour, I use the State pattern: one class per state. Illegal transitions are the missing cells, and they also become my test cases. Concurrent events need a lock or compare-and-set.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Transitions are event [guard] / action. For an order: CREATED to PAID or CANCELLED, PAID to SHIPPED or CANCELLED, SHIPPED to DELIVERED. Anything else is illegal and should throw or be ignored by explicit decision.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
enum OrderState {
    CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;
    boolean canGoTo(OrderState n) {
        return switch (this) {
            case CREATED -> n == PAID || n == CANCELLED;
            case PAID -> n == SHIPPED || n == CANCELLED;
            case SHIPPED -> n == DELIVERED;
            default -> false;
        };
    }
}
enum class OrderState {
    CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;
    fun canGoTo(n: OrderState) = when (this) {
        CREATED -> n == PAID || n == CANCELLED
        PAID -> n == SHIPPED || n == CANCELLED
        SHIPPED -> n == DELIVERED
        else -> false
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting illegal transitions and unexpected events.
  • Forgetting concurrency: two threads paying and cancelling at once.
  • Boolean flags (isPaid, isShipped) instead of a state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Enum or State pattern? -> Enum plus table for little behaviour; State classes when behaviour differs a lot per state.
  2. Concurrency? -> Lock per order, or UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'PAID' as compare-and-set.
  3. Big workflows? -> A state machine library or a persisted workflow engine.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE uses status strings and if. Senior uses a transition table, guards, atomic transition and tests every illegal cell.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payment callback and a user cancel raced and shipped a cancelled order; a conditional update on the state fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What does a use-case diagram show, and what is the difference between <<include>> and <<extend>>?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the requirements picture; the direction of include and extend is a common slip.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It shows who (actors) uses the system for what (use cases) and nothing about how. <<include>> means the base use case always runs another one, like Withdraw includes Authenticate PIN. <<extend>> is an optional addition, like Print receipt extending Deposit. Include arrow points to the included; extend arrow points to the base.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fast method: list actors in 30 seconds (humans and external systems like a payment gateway or scheduler), then 4 to 6 verbs per actor. Each oval later becomes a public method or a test case. Ride booking: Rider (request, cancel, rate), Driver (accept, start, end), Payment system (charge); requestRide(riderId, pickup, drop) is one oval.

Customer -> (Withdraw cash) --<<include>>--> (Authenticate PIN)
Customer -> (Deposit) <--<<extend>>-- (Print receipt)
Bank staff -> (Refill cash)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting database or class detail in it.
  • Reversing include and extend.
  • Forgetting external actors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do use cases appear in code? -> Service methods and acceptance tests.
  2. Is a user story the same? -> A textual use case.
  3. Use case vs sequence? -> Use case lists what; sequence shows one flow of how.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE draws ovals. Senior lists actors including systems, keeps it to what, and maps each oval to a method.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A missed "scheduler" actor meant nobody owned the nightly expiry job in the design.

questions.contextHtml: Interview prompt: "Library: members borrow books, max 5 books at a time, a fine applies after 14 days, a book can have several copies." You have 2 minutes at the whiteboard. The interviewer will next add "reserve a book that is out" and watch how your diagram absorbs it.
questions.promptHtml: Sketch the classes and relationships, and show how the new requirement fits.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Member holding List<Book> with due dates in a map, fine logic inside Member.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Several copies of the same title? Fine rate fixed or configurable? Can a member reserve while holding the max?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I write nouns first: Member, Book, Copy, Loan, Library, FinePolicy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Loan is an association class that holds dates (member and copy); Book is the title, Copy is the physical item; FinePolicy is an interface (varies).
  4. How I'd verify: Walk "borrow with 5 loans" and "return late" through the boxes.
  5. Root cause of common errors: Storing dates on Member or Book; fine logic inside Loan.
  6. Design: Member 1 --- * Loan * --- 1 Copy * --- 1 Book; Library coordinates; FinePolicy <<interface>> with DailyFine. Reservation: a new Reservation class (Member, Book, queue order) and the Library.return calls ReservationQueue; existing classes barely change.
Member 1 ---- * Loan * ---- 1 Copy * ---- 1 Book
Library 1 <#>-- * Copy
<<interface>> FinePolicy <|.. DailyFine      Loan ..> FinePolicy
Reservation * ---- 1 Book,  * ---- 1 Member
  1. Prevention: Mark multiplicities only where they matter; stop at 6 to 10 classes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No getters/setters, no User hierarchy (Member vs Librarian) unless asked.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fine differs by member type -> FinePolicy chosen by membership; seam already there.
  • Is Library composition over Copy? -> Yes if copies cannot exist without the library.
  • Where does the max-5 rule live? -> Library.borrow or a BorrowingPolicy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A design without an association class stored due dates in a map on Member; reservations later forced a rewrite.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Member holds everything.
  • Hire: Loan class, FinePolicy interface, correct multiplicities.
  • Strong hire: Book vs Copy, absorbs reservation with minimal change, narrates trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: Interviewer: "Show me what happens when a user places an order. Payment can fail." You have 1 minute. The participants are Client, Controller, OrderService, PaymentGateway, Repo. Your first attempt shows every internal call including logging and validation, and the diagram has 20 arrows.
questions.promptHtml: Redraw it so it makes the point, and map it to code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Draws 20 arrows with no failure path, mixing sync and async arrows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is payment synchronous? Should the order be saved before or after charging? What is the failure behaviour (no order, or a PENDING order)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut to the one happy path with 4 to 5 participants in call order and number the arrows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The question is about order of calls and the payment failure; internal logging is noise.
  4. How I'd verify: Check that the diagram answers "what if charge fails" with one alt box.
  5. Root cause of bad sketches: Drawing every call; forgetting return and failure paths.
  6. Diagram and code:
Client   Controller   OrderService   PaymentGateway   Repo
  1 placeOrder()-->
          2 create(o)--->
                      3 charge(card, 500)-->
                      <-- 4 ok
                      5 save(o)------------------------>
 <-- Order
alt [charge fails]: OrderService returns Error, no save

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Order place(Cart c) {
    payment.charge(c.card(), c.total());      // throws on failure: no save
    return repo.save(new Order(c));
}
fun place(c: Cart): Order { payment.charge(c.card, c.total); return repo.save(Order(c)) }
  1. Prevention: Always add the one main alt box; say what I skipped.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not saving before charging unless the interviewer wants a PENDING state; that adds a compensation story.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Charge succeeds but save fails -> need refund or an idempotent retry; mention it, then draw a second alt.
  • Payment is async via webhook -> open arrowhead and a callback participant; the order becomes PENDING.
  • Where is the transaction? -> Around save only; the charge is an external call.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A candidate who drew the save-after-charge order caught a missing refund path before coding started.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: 20 arrows, no failure.
  • Hire: ordered happy path with an alt box and code mapping.
  • Strong hire: raises save-failure after charge, async variant, narrates skipped parts.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders table shows 37 orders last week with state='CANCELLED' but a shipment was created. Logs for one of them:

10:01:02.113 payment-callback  order=881 load state=CREATED
10:01:02.115 cancel-api        order=881 load state=CREATED
10:01:02.140 payment-callback  order=881 set state=PAID  (canGoTo ok)
10:01:02.152 cancel-api        order=881 set state=CANCELLED (canGoTo ok)
10:01:03.001 shipper           order=881 saw PAID earlier -> shipment created

The code uses the enum canGoTo table from the state diagram; unit tests for every illegal transition pass.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more unit tests" or blame the shipper.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are state changes read-then-write in application code? Isolation level? Can the shipper be triggered from any state event?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Find the 37 orders, refund or stop shipments manually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lost update (both loaded CREATED); the transition table checks the in-memory state, not the stored state; the shipper acts on an event without re-validating.
  4. How I'd verify: The log timeline above shows both loads at CREATED before either write; reproduce with two threads in a test.
  5. Root cause: Check-then-act without atomicity. The diagram says what is legal, not who wins a race.
  6. Fix: Make the transition atomic.
UPDATE orders SET state = 'CANCELLED' WHERE id = 881 AND state IN ('CREATED','PAID');
-- affected rows = 0 means someone else moved it: reload and decide

Alternatively a version column or a per-order lock. The shipper verifies the state is still PAID at the time of shipping. 7. Prevention: A concurrency test using two threads for pay and cancel; metrics on rejected transitions. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No global lock; per-row conditional update is cheap and scalable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cancel after PAID needs refund -> the legal transition has an action; run it exactly once with an idempotency key.
  • Distributed services? -> The order service owns the state; others send commands, not set state.
  • Is PAID to CANCELLED then SHIPPED legal? -> No; encode it in the table and the guard.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cancel and a payment webhook raced about 40 times a week; a conditional update dropped the problem to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more unit tests only.
  • Hire: spots check-then-act, atomic update.
  • Strong hire: handles the downstream shipper, refund action, concurrency test.

questions.contextHtml: A checkout activity diagram shows "Charge card" (800 ms) and "Reserve stock" (300 ms) in parallel after "Validate cart", then "Send confirmation". The team implemented it with coroutineScope { async {charge}; async {reserve} }. In production, about 0.4% of orders end with the card charged but stock not reserved (out of stock race), and finance counts 120 such orders last month.
questions.promptHtml: What does the diagram miss, and how do you change the design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run them sequentially" with no thought about failure, or retry forever.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the charge refundable instantly? Can stock be reserved first at no cost? Is overselling acceptable for some items?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A reconciliation job refunding paid orders without a reservation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Parallel branches have no failure join: one succeeds while the other fails; no compensation action exists.
  4. How I'd verify: Query orders with a charge id and no reservation; check timing against stock-out spikes.
  5. Root cause: The activity diagram showed fork and join but no failure and compensation path.
  6. Fix: Reserve stock first (cheap, reversible: 300 ms), then charge (expensive); on charge failure release the reservation. Latency becomes 1,100 ms; or keep the parallel version and add compensation on the join.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Reservation r = inventory.reserve(cart);          // 300 ms, reversible
try { payment.charge(cart); }
catch (PaymentException e) { inventory.release(r); throw e; }
val r = inventory.reserve(cart)
try { payment.charge(cart) } catch (e: PaymentException) { inventory.release(r); throw e }
  1. Prevention: Every fork in a diagram gets a failure/compensation note; chaos test where one branch fails.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The sequential version costs 300 ms; I accept it unless the latency SLO says otherwise, then I keep parallel plus compensation. I would not leave failure unhandled.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reservation expires -> TTL on holds and a release job.
  • Refund also fails -> retry with idempotency, alert after N failures, manual queue.
  • Why not a distributed transaction? -> Payment gateways do not join your transaction; use sagas.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Parallelizing two calls saved 300 ms and created 120 manual refunds a month; reordering by "reversible first" fixed both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ignores partial failure.
  • Hire: compensation or reordering.
  • Strong hire: reversible-first principle, latency trade-off, saga mention.

questions.contextHtml:
A design doc diagram says Order <#>---- OrderLine (composition) and Team <>---- Player (aggregation). The code in the PR:

class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines;
    Order(List<OrderLine> lines) { this.lines = lines; }   // caller owns the list
}
class Team {
    private final List<Player> players = new ArrayList<>();
    Team(String name) { players.add(new Player("captain")); }
}

Another arrow in the doc shows Circle ----|> Shape with the arrowhead at Circle.
questions.promptHtml: Review the diagram against the code. What do you flag?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, diagrams are just rough sketches."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can an OrderLine exist without an Order? Do players move between teams?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the diagram or the code before the doc is used as a reference.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The notation is swapped (arrows reversed on inheritance; aggregation and composition mixed); code and diagram disagree on ownership.
  4. How I'd verify: Ask "does the part die with the whole?" and look at who creates it (new inside vs passed in).
  5. Root cause: Diagram drawn from memory, not from the code's ownership.
  6. Findings: Order takes lines from outside, so in code it is aggregation, though the intent is composition (lines die with the order): fix code by creating or copying lines inside. Team creates players inside, so code is composition but the domain says players are free agents: change code to receive players. Circle ----|> Shape must have the arrowhead at the parent Shape.
  7. Prevention: Generate diagrams from code in CI (PlantUML/Mermaid checked into the repo) or review them with the PR.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not argue notation purity; the point is ownership and lifecycle agree.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Defensive copy for composition? -> new ArrayList<>(lines) prevents the caller mutating shared state.
  • Do diagrams matter if code is the truth? -> They matter for communication; stale ones are worse than none.
  • Realization arrow? -> Dashed line with hollow triangle to the interface.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A wrong ownership arrow led to two services sharing a mutable list and a heisenbug; the lifecycle question caught it in review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: skims the diagram.
  • Hire: finds reversed arrow and ownership mismatch.
  • Strong hire: connects it to defensive copies and proposes diagram-in-repo.

questions.contextHtml: Prompt: "Design a ride-booking backend." The interviewer says only that riders request rides and drivers accept. Your first use-case diagram has Rider and Driver. Later in the interview the interviewer asks "who triggers payment after the trip, who expires an unaccepted request after 2 minutes, and who handles support refunds?" and your design has no owner for these.
questions.promptHtml: How should you have scoped the use cases, and how do you patch the design now?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "I will add them as methods on Rider."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which systems act without a human (payment gateway, scheduler, notification service)? Is support in scope? Do drivers and riders share an account model?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the missing actors now and re-state scope.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Only human actors were listed; external systems (Payment, Scheduler) and Support were forgotten.
  4. How I'd verify: For each state change in the lifecycle (requested, accepted, started, ended, paid, expired), ask "who or what triggers it?".
  5. Root cause: Use-case discovery stopped at the first two humans.
  6. Fix: Actors: Rider (request, cancel, rate), Driver (accept, start, end), Payment system (charge, refund callback), Scheduler (expire request after 2 min), Support agent (refund). Each oval becomes a service method; expiry becomes a scheduled job on RideService.expireStale() and an entry in the ride state machine.
Rider    -> request ride, cancel, rate
Driver   -> accept, start trip, end trip
Payment  -> charge fare, refund
Scheduler-> expire stale requests (2 min)
Support  -> issue refund
  1. Prevention: Checklist: humans, external systems, time-based triggers.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not design support tooling in depth unless asked; mark it out of scope.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Scheduler fails -> idempotent expiry plus a periodic sweep.
  • Rider and Driver are both Users? -> One User with roles, or separate types; ask about cross-role use.
  • Include vs extend for "apply promo"? -> Extend: optional addition to request ride.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A design with no scheduler actor leaked "searching" rides forever until someone asked who ends them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: two actors only.
  • Hire: adds systems and scheduler once prompted.
  • Strong hire: finds them up front using the trigger question.

questions.contextHtml: A diagram for "upload photo" shows Client, API, Storage, Thumbnailer, Notifier with all solid arrows. In production, uploads of 8 MB take 6 s end to end because the API waits for thumbnail generation (4 s) and the push notification (500 ms) before replying. The SLO is a 1 s response. Thumbnailer fails about 1% of the time and the client sees errors even though the photo was stored.
questions.promptHtml: Redraw the sequence to meet the SLO and say how it changes the code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a bigger server" or just change arrows without handling failure and status.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the thumbnail exist when the response returns? Is eventual consistency okay? How does the client learn it is ready?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make thumbnail failures non-fatal to the upload response.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Synchronous chain; the notifier and thumbnailer are not on the critical path; failures propagate to the client.
  4. How I'd verify: Trace spans per hop: Storage 700 ms, Thumbnailer 4 s, Notifier 500 ms.
  5. Root cause: All calls drawn and implemented as synchronous.
  6. Fix: Sequence: Client -> API: upload; API -> Storage: put (solid, waits); API -> Queue: enqueue(thumbnail job) (async, open arrowhead); API -> Client: 202 with photo id. Worker: Queue -> Thumbnailer -> Storage; Worker -> Notifier. Client polls or receives a push when ready. Failed jobs retry with a dead-letter queue.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
String upload(byte[] data) {
    String id = storage.put(data);              // sync, 700 ms
    queue.publish(new ThumbnailJob(id));        // async, returns fast
    return id;
}
fun upload(data: ByteArray): String { val id = storage.put(data); queue.publish(ThumbnailJob(id)); return id }
  1. Prevention: Mark sync vs async arrows distinctly; keep SLO budget per hop in the design.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The user may see a photo without a thumbnail briefly; show a placeholder. Not using fire-and-forget threads without a durable queue (jobs are lost on a crash).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicate job delivery -> thumbnail generation must be idempotent by photo id.
  • Notification must be exactly once? -> Not guaranteed; dedupe key per photo.
  • Large files? -> Direct-to-storage presigned upload (verify provider specifics).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A synchronous chain of four services turned a 700 ms upload into 6 s; moving two hops behind a queue returned it to 800 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales hardware.
  • Hire: async queue for non-critical hops with a 202 response.
  • Strong hire: idempotent workers, DLQ, distinguishes arrows and budgets latency.

questions.contextHtml: 45-minute LLD round for a parking lot. At minute 12 you are still polishing a class diagram with 14 classes, getters and setters, and visibility marks on every field. The interviewer glances at the clock: no code yet. At minute 14 they add: "And pricing should differ for weekends." You notice the diagram does not show where that fits.
questions.promptHtml: Recover the round: what do you cut, what do you say, and where does the weekend rule go?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps polishing, or throws the diagram away and starts coding without a model.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is weekend pricing the only variation, or will other rules come? Should I code the core flow or the pricing first?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop drawing, say "I will stop at the current diagram and mark what I skipped".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: I over-invested in notation; getters, setters and field details are not what is being judged.
  4. How I'd verify: Check the diagram has 6 to 8 key classes and one sequence for "park a car".
  5. Root cause: No time box, drawing without narration.
  6. Fix: Cut getters/setters, collapse minor classes, add <<interface>> PricingStrategy with HourlyPricing and WeekendPricing in about 10 seconds (the diagram shows the seam). Draw a 1.5-minute sequence of park, then say what I skipped and start coding the core classes. Aim for about 25 minutes of code.
ParkingLot 1 <#>-- * Floor 1 <#>-- * Slot
ParkingLot ..> Ticket        <<interface>> PricingStrategy <|.. HourlyPricing, WeekendPricing
sequence: Vehicle -> ParkingLot.park -> Floor.findSlot -> Ticket
  1. Prevention: Fixed budget: use-cases 1 min, class diagram 2 min, sequence 1.5, state 1 if a lifecycle exists.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No perfecting notation, no silent drawing; I would not skip the diagram altogether, it prevents mid-code confusion.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer wants a state diagram -> one for Ticket: ACTIVE to PAID to EXITED, 1 minute.
  • Mermaid allowed? -> Fine if quick; keep the same notation throughout.
  • Another requirement in minute 30 -> point at the seam in the diagram and add one class.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A candidate who spent 15 minutes on UML never reached the concurrency discussion; the next candidate drew 6 classes in 4 minutes and spent the time on seat locking.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps polishing, no code.
  • Hire: cuts detail, adds the seam, moves to code.
  • Strong hire: narrates skipped parts, time budget, links boxes to classes.
